opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a genuinely hard problem, but maybe not as hard as people sometimes assume. The thing to remember is that frontier AI development, at least the way it's currently done, has a very large physical footprint. You need enormous numbers of specialised chips, data centres drawing hundreds of megawatts of power, cooling infrastructure, and so on. That's quite different from, say, trying to verify a ban on bioweapons research, where the relevant work could happen in a small lab almost anywhere.

So one natural starting point is compute. The cutting-edge chips come through a remarkably narrow supply chain: a handful of companies designing them, essentially one company fabricating the most advanced ones, and a few firms making the lithography machines needed to produce them. That gives you chokepoints where you could track how many chips are being made and where they end up. You could imagine something like the IAEA's approach to fissile material, with an accounting of where the compute is and inspections to check that it's still there and being used for what's been declared.

Then you can go further with hardware-level mechanisms. There's been interesting work on chips that could attest to what they're doing, or that require some kind of licence to run large training workloads, or that report their location. None of that is fully mature, and you'd have to worry about tampering, but it's the kind of thing that could be built in if both sides wanted verification to work.

There are also cruder signals that are hard to hide. Large training runs consume enormous amounts of electricity and generate a lot of heat, so national technical means like satellite imagery and power grid monitoring can tell you a fair bit. Each country already watches the other closely, and that existing intelligence capacity gives some baseline assurance.

Where it gets harder is that the picture could change. If algorithmic efficiency keeps improving, the amount of compute needed to reach a given capability level falls, and the footprint shrinks. And an agreement that only limits training doesn't necessarily cover what you can do by scaling up inference, which is more spread out and looks more like ordinary commercial use. So any verification regime would need to be updated as the technology moves, and probably needs to focus on the largest concentrations of compute rather than trying to police everything.

I'd also stress that verification doesn't need to be perfect to be valuable. With arms control during the Cold War, the US and Soviet Union didn't have perfect insight into each other's programmes. What mattered was that cheating at a scale that would really shift the strategic balance was likely to be detected. If you can get to a point where a secret project large enough to matter would probably be caught, that might be enough for both sides to prefer the agreement to an unconstrained race. And the political will is really the binding constraint here. If both governments came to see racing as more dangerous than restraint, I think the technical side of verification is something we could work out.

r001.rationale: The response mentions chips that could report their location, but does not say they would stop operating if the location signal were blocked.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss visibly dismantling nuclear bombers or using that to verify destruction of military capacity.

r003.rationale: The response says verification may be less difficult than assumed and could be worked out, but does not argue that declaring it impossible after very little investigation is premature.

r004.rationale: It does not explain that reciprocal destruction could make destroying one’s own already-built capacity worthwhile.

r005.rationale: It proposes no reciprocal destruction of equivalent US and Chinese GPU capacity.

r006.rationale: It proposes no internationally supervised escrow for US and Chinese GPU capacity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the things I'm most interested in at the moment, because I think it's actually a lot more tractable than people assume, and the reason is that the key input here is physical. If you look at the history of arms control, nuclear arms control in particular, the thing that made it work wasn't trust between the superpowers — there wasn't much of that — it was that the thing you cared about was countable and hard to hide. Warheads, delivery vehicles, enrichment facilities. You could put inspectors on the ground, you could use satellites, you could use seismic monitoring for tests. And AI has a surprisingly similar structure, in that the frontier is bottlenecked on compute.

So if you want to train a model that's substantially beyond the current frontier, you need tens of thousands of cutting-edge chips, running together in a single facility for months, consuming on the order of hundreds of megawatts of power. That's not something you can do in a basement. These data centres are enormous, they have very distinctive thermal signatures, and they're visible from orbit. So a lot of the verification can actually be done remotely, which is politically very attractive, because the sticking point in these negotiations is usually that neither side wants the other's inspectors wandering around their sensitive facilities.

Then the second layer is the supply chain. There are really only a handful of chokepoints — ASML for the lithography equipment, TSMC for the fabrication, Nvidia and a couple of others for the design — and those chips are already tracked quite closely because of export controls. So you could imagine an agreement that includes a registry of where high-end chips go, with both sides able to audit that. And beyond that, there's been quite a lot of technical work on what you might call on-chip verification: mechanisms where the hardware itself can attest to what it's being used for, or where chips need to periodically check in with some kind of licensing authority to keep operating. None of that's deployed at the moment, and there are real questions about whether it can be made tamper-resistant, but it's not science fiction either.

The thing I'd stress is that you don't need perfect verification. You need enough that cheating at a scale that actually matters would be detected with high probability. If China or the US secretly ran a slightly-larger-than-permitted training run, that's not catastrophic. What you want to rule out is a secret run ten or a hundred times larger than the agreed limit, and that's exactly the thing that's hardest to hide, because the energy and the hardware footprint scale with it.

Where I think it gets genuinely difficult is on the algorithmic side. If compute efficiency keeps improving, then a limit expressed in terms of chips or floating-point operations gets looser in effect every year, so any agreement would need some mechanism for ratcheting the thresholds down over time. And there's the question of what happens if the bottleneck shifts away from training towards inference or towards running lots of copies of a model, which is much more distributed and much harder to monitor. So I don't want to pretend it's solved. But compared to, say, verifying a bioweapons agreement, where the relevant equipment fits in a small lab, I think AI is actually on the more verifiable end of the spectrum, and that's a reason for some hope.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing to say is that verification doesn’t have to be perfect. It needs to make a substantial violation sufficiently difficult, and sufficiently likely to be detected, that neither side thinks it’s worth trying.

One promising approach would be to focus on computing power. If you’re trying to verify what algorithms someone has developed, or what capabilities a system has, that’s quite difficult. But the largest training runs require physical infrastructure: a lot of specialised chips, in data centres, using substantial amounts of electricity. That gives you something more tangible to monitor.

You could imagine an agreement that required registration of the largest computing facilities, reporting of training runs above some threshold, and inspections to check that those reports were accurate. You might also have technical mechanisms for checking how chips are being used without revealing all of the commercially sensitive information involved.

But I wouldn’t want to suggest that this is a solved problem. You’d have to consider whether training could be distributed across facilities, whether chips could be diverted, and how improvements in algorithms might undermine a limit expressed purely in terms of computing power.

So I’d see verification as a research programme that we should be pursuing now. Even if the US and China aren’t ready to make an agreement, having credible ways to verify one could make an enormous difference when they are.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that verification doesn’t have to be perfect to be useful. It has to give each side enough confidence that the other couldn’t gain a large advantage without a substantial risk of being caught.

One possibility is to focus on the physical infrastructure needed to train the most powerful systems. Software is quite difficult to monitor, but very large concentrations of specialised chips, and the power and cooling infrastructure that go with them, are more tangible. You could imagine an agreement involving declarations of major computing facilities, some form of inspection, and monitoring of the use of the chips themselves.

But there are real difficulties. You’d need to distinguish prohibited development from permitted uses of the same hardware, protect commercially and militarily sensitive information, and account for improvements in algorithms that let people do more with less computing power. So a limit on computing power wouldn’t be a perfect limit on capability.

I’d want technical experts to investigate how much assurance different arrangements could actually provide. The encouraging point is that the two countries wouldn’t necessarily have to trust each other’s intentions. They’d need a verification system that made a consequential violation sufficiently difficult to conceal.
